utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Today Monday, the 28th of August, 2006. I would like to greet never have I one in the courtroom. As you will be aware, we are continuing our work today and we are continuing with a witness who has already been heard. He appeared before the Court recess. I'd like to remind you of something though. The Prosecution has taken up two hours and 33 minutes, which means that they have between an hour and a half and two hours left. Having noted that, we made certain calculations regarding the cross-examination, and the results are as follows: For each accused, for Mr. Praljak's Defence, one hour and 30 minutes; for Mr. Petkovic Defence, an hour and 30 minutes; for Mr. Stojic's Defence, one and a half hours; for Mr. Pusic's Defence 45 minutes; for Mr. Coric's Defence 45 minutes, and for Mr. Prlic's defence, 45 minutes. We took into consideration the principle of flexibility when calculating the time they should have and the necessity each accused had to present their Defence case. As a result we gave more time three of the accused than the other three since the testimony of (redacted) relates more directly to these witnesses. And secondly, I learned yesterday that the Prosecution made a motion to have 380-odd documents admitted for Witness Beese. Having cast a rapid glance at the Prosecution's submission, at the Prosecution's motion, it was possible to conclude that the motion did not correspond to the guidelines in a decision of ours. We explained that in order to request the admission of certain documents, certain criteria had to be met. One had to treat the matter criteria by criteria, apparently, a certain number of criteria had not been referred to in the Prosecution's motion, and that at least concerns why the documents are necessary. And as a result, if nothing is amended, it's very likely that this motion will be rejected. If Judges take very precise decisions, it's because this is all part of a general framework, note the good administration of justice. On a number of occasions, the Trial Chamber has noted that the Prosecution fails to comply with the -- our guidelines, with our requests, and in particular concerns Rule 65 ter. We're waiting for your submissions in September. If you had met the requests previously made, we would have been able to avoid a certain number of problems. I would also like to remind you of the fact that the parties can make suggestions, but it's the Judges who are -- finally take the decisions that are relevant. It is not the other way around. Tomorrow we will be rendering a decision concerning documents that concern last week's witness. We'll render this decision in the presence of the registrar, who is not here today, but he will be present tomorrow. We'll render our decision when he is present here tomorrow. It is not necessary to render the decision today. The matter is not that urgent. Having said that, we may now continue with hearing Witness BJ. As the blinds have been lowered, we can now call Witness BJ into the courtroom. And since protective measures had been granted to this witness, we'll be proceeding with the hearing of this witness now. Could the usher please call the witness into the courtroom now. And I'd also like the registrar to make an order so that a certain matter can be amended. I think that's why Mr. Murphy is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I had a slightly different matter to deal with briefly which I could address while the witness is being brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, on Friday we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: -- we received a letter from the Prosecution indicating their intention to use an exhibit with this witness. The number for of the exhibit for the record is P 03545, which they said was inadvertently not included on the list of exhibits concerning the present witness. Your Honour, for the record, we object to this document now being produced and used. It's a document of great significance, and we object to its late use in the manner the Prosecution proposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, I have just learned about a problem. According to the Defence, there is a document that you would like to use. This document was not part of the list of documents that the Defence had to be provided with prior to the beginning of the cross-examination and the examination-in-chief. According to the Defence, this is your responsibility. You made this mission take. You forgot to produce or, rather, list this document. I don't have the document before me, so it's impossible for me to assess how important this document is. What could you tell us about the reasons for wanting to use this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Might I be able to address before that the question of the motion concerning the ECMM documents and the Witness Beese. We will certainly review our filing, Your Honour. We don't know, based on the court's comments, exactly which criteria you are concerned about, but we will certainly be reviewing that this afternoon to see where we are, and perhaps we can take those matters up with your legal officer staff to determine what the concerns are more specifically. We did indicate in our filing that because the larger filing that is due on the 4th of September, a few days from now, since that filing was imminent and since, as you might understand, the Office of the Prosecutor is devoting a huge amount of resources to the finalisation of those charts which are quite voluminous, we felt that some of the criteria indicated in the Chamber's guidance concerning the ECMM documents would be covered by the ECMM chart, and it was a matter of essentially duplicating effort within a few days of each other. But having said that, Your Honour, we'll be happy of course to review our filing further and see if we can identify the Chamber's further concerns about that. In connection with this witness and specifically Exhibit 3545, Your Honour, it was in our existing 65 ter exhibit list. It was handed out to the Chamber when the witness, Witness BJ, was here in June of this year. It was noted again to the Defence recently that we were going to use the document. We said in our letter that it was inadvertent, and, Your Honour, when one is dealing with this many documents, it is not -- it probably won't be unusual, to be perfectly honest, for a document to be left off a list from time to time given the volume of material that we're dealing with. And it was simply that. I can tell you that it's been in my outline since day one since I began preparing for this witness before he came in June, and it's always been our intention to use the document, and again as we said, it was inadvertently found not to be on the witness list for this witness but certainly was on our Rule 65 ter list that we filed in June -- sorry, January. Once we determined that it wasn't on the list and reviewing and preparing for this session, obviously we've been doing a lot between the time that the witness was first here and today, and when we began to prepare again at the end of last week for this witness, it then appeared to us that the document was not on the list that had been given to the Defence, and that is why at the earliest opportunity sent the letter to the Defence to notify them of the omission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, if I have understood you correctly, you are saying that this document, 3545, is in the chart which includes a summary of the testimony. However, there was a material omission that was committed when you forwarded the complete list or the full list of documents to the Defence, apparently this is something that you forgot.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think that's correct. I mean, as I understand what the Court has just said, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Murphy, the Prosecution has just said that the Defence initially knew that a certain witness would be heard and that there were certain documents that concerned the witness. This is in conformity with 65 ter, the Rule 65 ter. And then in the list that was provided a few days before the witness appeared, a mistake was made and something was omitted. So it's not a document that has appeared out of the blue. A reference has already been made to this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- I think I'm right in saying that it was not in the chart with the summary of the testimony. It may well have been in the original 65 ter exhibit list. I don't have that in front of me, but I think that Mr. Scott would confirm that it was not on the chart summarising the witness's testimony. If I'm wrong, I'll be corrected about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, no. We've been quite transparent, I think. On the most recent chart that was handed out in connection with the witness closest in time to his previous appearance, it was not on the list. However, it has twice before been disclosed. It was disclosed first of all in January in our Rule 65 ter exhibit list. It was also disclosed specifically connected to this witness in April of 2006. The Chamber will recall that as an interim measure when the full charts had not been prepared, Your Honour directed us to prepare certain charts for the first groups of witnesses, and that was done and that was filed in April. I don't have the exact date in front of me, but that was filed in April. And I'm now looking at the screen of an electronic copy of that chart that was filed in April, and indeed Exhibit 3545 is specifically listed specifically in connection with this witness. So again, Your Honour, I repeat that it was inadvertently omitted from the third disclosure document but disclosed in the first two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Judges, having deliberated, believe that the Prosecution should be allowed to use this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, first of all I would like to greet you on behalf of all of the Judges. You are receiving the interpretation in your own language of what I'm saying, as well as the interpretation of what the parties are saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. Yes, indeed, Your Honour. I can hear perfectly well in my own language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir. I will now give the floor to Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness BJ.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I would like to also remind you, you are testifying under certain protective measures, that is, you have been given the pseudonym BJ, and we will not be referring to you by name. You've also been provided the protective measure of having your facial image blurred or obstructed so that your face is not broadcast outside the courtroom. I will also caution you, sir, that if you give certain testimony that is very specific to yourself that may tend to identify you, I ask you to think about that and exercise some caution, and I will do and do the same. Thank you. Witness, we left off from your testimony in the latter part of June of this year talking about the humanitarian situation in East Mostar in the early summer of 1993. And to begin on that again, sir, I would like to direct your attention. If the witness could please be shown Exhibit P 01717, which is the operations -- I'll remind everyone in the courtroom is the operations logbook. I think, Your Honour, what we did the last time this witness was here was he was provided a hard copy set of the Spanish language materials which facilitated him being able to work with the material most efficiently. I would suggest that we do that again if the Court agrees. With the usher's assistance, we will provide him -- we've given in hard copy as well. Our experience last time was it was helpful for him to have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you're going to have in front of you now at least what I can see the document electronically in the Spanish language. You've also been provided a binder with various hard copy documents in them. I leave it to you to decide how -- what's most helpful to you in working with the Spanish language version of the documents. I suspect that most of the other people in the courtroom will be looking at either the English or the B/C/S versions. Perhaps not. Sir, if you have your -- the logbook, P 01717, if I could direct your attention using the numbers on the upper right corner the page, in the Spanish version it would be at R0167850. In the English version, I believe you will find it -- those in the courtroom will find it at page 113. Do you have that, sir? Entry for the 17th of July, 1993. 17 July 1993. The English version starting on the bottom of page 113. Yes. Electronically it's in front of you now also, I believe.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. I do have them right in front of me. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, on the 17th of July, 1993, there is the following, and I will review it with you and then I'll ask you a few questions about it. "All movement of UNPROFOR vehicles remain prohibited in the direction of Mostar and Capljina. Intense fighting continued in the Mostar area increasing, in particular, at the southern entrance to the city. Buna is the confrontation line between the two sides. Radio contact was established with the BH inside the city. They reported that the situation was critical. There was a shortage of food, medicines. For some days now they have -- they had had no water and electricity. The number of explosions in the town of Jablanica went down today. Passage remained denied to all UNPROFOR vehicles in any direction that would require them to pass through G. Dreznica," which may be Gorani Dreznica but I leave the note to you. "A reconnaissance patrol was carried out in the Jablanica- Kostajnica area. They reported that the area is calm. UNHCR suspended all the convoys because the HVO demanded that a certain percentage of aid be distributed to both communities before authorising passage through their territory." Now, sir, I direct your attention first of all to the date, 17th of July, 1993. And just to summarise or if we can say catch up again with the testimony that you gave in June, did the Spanish Battalion of UNPROFOR have access to the city of Mostar? Were you actually able to go into the city of Mostar on the 17th of July, or in that time period, of 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we were not able to go into the city of Mostar on that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And during this time --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand that when I say -- are you talking about the -- are you talking about the Muslim side or the Croatian side of the city of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In particular, the city -- the part of East Mostar where most of the Muslim population was located.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were not able to go in.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, approximately -- can you remind us during approximate -- what a period of time -- excuse me, what period of time was that the case? From approximately when to when was the Spanish Battalion blocked for barred from going into the Muslim part of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to look it up in the logbook, but personally I would say about a month. But I'm being rather bold here in putting forward 30 days, but I would say somewhere between 20 and 30 days. But if you want me to I can look it up and give you the exact detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think, sir, that will be stated in the documents that are either already available to the Chamber or will be available to the Chamber. Can I ask you this: During the time when the Spanish Battalion was barred from the city, what was the principal means, if any, by which the Spanish Battalion was receiving information or reports of what was happening in the Mostar part of the town -- excuse me, the Muslim part of the town at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had radio contact with the Muslim side of Mostar, and we had such reports which reached us from the Muslims in Jablanica where we had a detachment in contact with them, and they got information from the Muslims from Jablanica. And those Muslims from Jablanica did have contact with the Muslims in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Apart from the -- yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is something I would like to clarify, something that I believe is important. The question/answer, is somewhat confusing or gives rise to a question. In the first line it says the movement of UNPROFOR vehicles was prohibited. It said all movement of these vehicles should continue to be prohibited. So you could not circulate because of the shots. That's what it says in the first line of the document. Was it because the BH, the ABiH, or the HVO said you did not have the right to circulate in the area? What was the main reason for this prohibition.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, any time we tried to move towards Capljina or towards Mostar, we came up against HVO checkpoints preventing us from proceeding forward. Whenever we engaged in authorisations that we tried to obtain from HVO, it would take forever, forever. In fact, they actually told us we cannot go anywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And within your mandate, given your mandate, were you free to move around or did you have to stop at checkpoints according to the mandate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to the UN Resolution that is quite true, but in practice it was an entirely different story. We did not have that freedom of movement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But when the problem arose on the first day, they didn't authorise you to circulate. Were the HVO authorities informed by your heads of the problem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Affirmative. That is quite true. We did get in touch with the headquarters of the HVO. We told them that we are blocked, that there was a checkpoint at this particular point on the road, that we were impeded in our movement forward. We asked them to get in touch with the people manning that checkpoint to ask them to authorise us to proceed, but in practice that authorisation never came. They actually said, "You can't move," but in the end there was never an answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But when HVO controlled you, were they soldiers who were armed or was it a matter of tanks? Because you had armoured vehicles, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it seems a little bit preposterous to say so here, but an army with armoured vehicles like ours, we were much stronger and we couldn't move but we were not authorized to resort to force. And any man with a Kalashnikov and a couple of mines could say, No, you can't move any more, and we couldn't use our own force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But if there's a soldier with a Kalashnikov at a checkpoint that you have an armoured vehicle at your disposal, you can move on. What could such a soldier do with his weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you see, there may have been mines hidden on the road. The road may have been mined. Anti-tank mines. So we would have had to get town from the tank, actually try and locate the mines, remove the mines and all of that under enemy fire. Perhaps -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would like to go a bit back to the contacts you had with authorities. You said that the headquarters of HVO was informed of such incidents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is so. Every time we were stopped at a checkpoint and we couldn't proceed, we had contact lines with the HVO headquarters. We informed the headquarters of the incident. We were told that we would be phoned up to try to solve the problem. And after a couple of hours they would phone back saying that we could not proceed because there was combat ahead. They always gave us a thousand different excuses to stop us at that particular checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... any names of persons with whom you had contacts or who were named to you as those making the decisions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We normally at the headquarters had a liaison officer. I phoned very many times Mr. Bozic who was the person whom I maintained most contacts. Not just myself, last the Spanish Battalion members. He was in some way the person who was in charge of solving problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was deputy minister of defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps while the transcript is still on our screens, on page 13, line 2, I think there's something missing. The negative is missing there, because the witness said that the HVO did not say that they were not to pass through but they never actually could. So there's the "not" that's missing there, I think.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this a question? Yes. They never said we could not go on. We just never could go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if we could also, in terms of transcript I believe this was corrected the last -- during your last prior testimony, on page 14, line 9, we have the reference in the transcript to Mr. Bosik [as interpreted] which is now spelled Bosik. Your Honour, from my review of the transcript of the prior testimony it was previously confirmed that was Slobodan Bozic, B-o-z- i-c. If we could have that correction, please. Sir, Mr. Bozic was your principal interlocutor in terms of the HVO during your tour in Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. It wasn't always him because very often duties, of course, prevented him from taking phone calls, but he was normally the most efficacious person who could solve things and cooperation with him was fairly good. They tried to cooperate and we always managed to talk to him whenever we managed to talk to him, he always tried to solve things but throughout that time we could never in fact achieve freedom of movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Am my follow-up question to you. Apart from Mr. Bozic, do you remember anyone else that you had regular contact with? By that I mean more than once or twice, but was there another person at HVO headquarters other than Mr. Bozic that you had any regular dealings with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember a couple of officers from the HVO, but I do not recall their names, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, the note -- the entry in the logbook that I directed your attention to a few moments ago included this particular passage, it says: "Passage remained denied to all UNPROFOR vehicles in any direction that would require them to pass through G. Dreznica." And I realise this is some time ago, but do you recall any information today about why that particular location appears to have been problematic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, right now I would have to see the map of Bosnia, locate Dreznica. I think that it was an obligated way to go somewhere else, but I cannot quite recall. I think that we had to go through Dreznica to go somewhere else, hence why we could not proceed through Dreznica. But quite clearly I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Further on in the passage you say that: "UNHCR suspended all the convoys." Can you explain to the Judges what the relationship was, if any, between UNHCR's humanitarian convoy work and the mission of the Spanish Battalion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main SpaBat mission in the area was to escort humanitarian aid convoys in the area. Within the area and also for all other convoys travelling towards Sarajevo and Central Bosnia. That was our main mission, our main duty, and everything was aimed at being able to escort those convoys. Our efforts were aimed at so doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just following up on the question that the president asked you for moments ago, when you not just you personally when the Spanish Battalion had the mandate to escort the humanitarian convoys, did your rules of engagement allow you to use armed force for those convoys to get through if they were blocked or impeded in some way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We could defend the convoy, but we could not force our way through. If the convoy came under threat or if the UNHCR personnel came under threat, we would defend both the convoy and the people, but to force our way through a blockade of the HVO's or whoever was not part of our mandate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could I ask you, sir, to next go to Exhibit P 03597. And for the courtroom, those using the hard copy bundles, it will be in the second bundle. 3797. I'm sorry. My apology. 3597. My mistake. 3597. I believe it is on page 8 of the English version and page 3 of the Spanish version, sir. And there --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. Excuse me. I have not been able to locate the document yet because you are speaking too far away from the microphone and the interpreters cannot hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it's difficult with the courtroom configuration as everyone knows. It's 3597, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date. Perhaps you could tell me the date of the document I would be able to locate it better.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Okay. The 21st of July, 1993. It's your intrep number 239.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: 17th of July you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My date indicates the 21st of July, sir. And I think we do have it on the document in front of -- on the electronic version.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, on page 8 of that document, sir, I believe -- well, in the English version and page 3 of the Spanish version, I believe you'll find the -- an entry, an that says the following: "1. BH army sources reported that the civilian population in Mostar is in a critical situation. There is not enough food and there is still no water or electricity. The hospital lacks medicines, anaesthetics and other items essential for treating the wounded from the fighting. However, they said that their morale was high and that they were prepared to defend their part of Mostar at all cost." This again is the 21st of July, 1993. And also following up again on questions that have been put to you by the Judges, do you recall whether the Spanish battalion was making continuing efforts during this time period to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Scott. I think we do not see this text in the document the way you have quoted it. You said you quoted from number 1?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On my document, page 8, there is a (1), but maybe my -- maybe somebody's given me the correct me if I'm wrong document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's under "Other information," so it would be on page 8 as opposed to page 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But before that, I was -- my attention was drawn to the first document. Can we go to the very top of the document, please. The beginning of the document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The previous page, the page we were looking at a moment ago. No, after that. I would like to see the page that we had on our screens before Judge Trechsel intervened. Yes. No. No, that's not it. The next page.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that is the last paragraph of the page that was on our screens a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's it. Scroll down to the beginning, please. No, up. Yes. Right. Now, Witness BJ, can you read the first paragraph that starts with the number 2 underneath the "Confidential" stamp? Can you read that sentence out to us, please, so that the interpreters can interpret it? It's number 2, and it says "Segun fuentes BiH," et cetera. Can you read that out in your own language.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the witness, please. Microphone. The interpreters cannot hear the witness, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "HVO sources, reliable sources at that, informed us that today with no opposition, the Cilu [as interpreted] village was occupied. Apparently, the HV forces heard a message whereby the village was being abandoned. When the troops were withdrawing and before the BSA," -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no. Can we go back to the document again, and I'm going to ask Madam Usher to leave that portion of the document on our screens and don't touch it any more. Now, would you read the first paragraph right at the top. It says number 2, and then number 3. Read number 2. The top of the page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "According to HV sources [as interpreted], amongst the prisoners of war captured, there is an HV colonel."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, my question is about that. What does that paragraph actually mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember this specific case, but what it means from what I can gather is that a colonel was captured, a Croat colonel, not from the HVO but from the Croat army. But I don't recall the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Mr. Scott, please proceed. One more question from the Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you. Previously, you have mentioned, sir, that in many instances when you tried to deliver to civilian population the assistance which they needed, you were stopped by -- by the HVO, and there was a request or a demand to -- to share with their own population or people as a kind of 50/50 arrangement. So my question is if it happened or not. That is my first question. The second question, that your assistance which you were supposed to deliver to the civilian population, was it earmarked for a particular group of people, for example, civilian population in Mostar or East Mostar, or it was a kind of general assistance to deliver to certain major areas? And my third question is that has it happened any time then you might have accepted the urgent requirement which was submitted to you by the HVO checkpoints that you have shared the assistance which you were delivering to the civilian population? So I may repeat the first question to be quite clear, that did it happen in practice that you -- you gave, let's say 50 per cent of your assistance to certain -- through certain checkpoints to the respective people, let's say Croats or Bosniaks or anybody who lived there? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. We did not distribute humanitarian aid to the civilian population. We escorted the UNHCR convoys, and it was this organisation that decided where aid was going to go. But, and I can give you a very clear example from a later time however, I can give an example then of the following: When negotiations were undertaken in order to let the convoys through, the HVOs always demanded that humanitarian aid be forwarded to both Croat and Muslim areas but we never had to leave humanitarian aid in situ. But before the convoy was led through the HVO demanded that their refugees received aid too. I don't know whether I have answered all three questions of yours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it seems to be there is a misunderstanding in the transcript again, because we had the document in Spanish on our monitors. I think that we ought to have the English version of the text, because the witness is looking at the original documents in Spanish in front of him. So I think we should have either English or French on our screens, the two official languages. And now I see on page 19, line 18, when the witness read out paragraph 2 that we're looking at on our screens, the witness quite literally, according to the transcript said: "According to HV sources, among the prisoners of war there was one HV colonel." That's what it says in the transcript. Now, what we can see on the monitor, on the document, as far as I know -- can read Spanish, the witness said, "According to BH sources," whereas in the transcript it appears to be the HV. So it would appear that they were HV sources. But we'll come to my later queries during the cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The witness said, according to BH sources, BiH sources, not HV source. So there was a mistake in the transcript there. But anyway, it would be visible that if the witness has the documents in Spanish, that those of us who do not know Spanish can look at the documents in English and in French, and I think that technically it is possible to have two documents on our screens, half/half, half the screen with the Spanish document and half the screen with the English version. We have them now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Scott, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We'll try to work with both documents side by side as much as possible, although sometimes when we put them side by side the text becomes fairly small, but we'll try it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, going back to the part of the document that I had referred you to some moments ago, which was on page 8 of the English version, and it's -- I see it's directly -- I see on the electronic version, it says, "BH sources reported that the civilian population in Mostar is in a critical situation. There is not enough food and there is still no water or electricity. The hospital lacks medicines, anaesthetics and other items essential for treating the wounded from the fighting. However, they said that their morale was high and that they were prepared to defend their part of Mostar at all cost." Can we understand then, sir, that based on your previous testimony most of these communications from the Muslim part of Mostar were coming via the radio during this period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of the information came via our radio at Medjugorje, but we also had information sources through Jablanica in the Muslim area and through the Muslims therein. Mostar and Jablanica were in fact linked through hills. There was, in fact, a corridor as it were. That's how we reached one place or the other. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you please, sir to go next to Exhibit P 03705.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And while that's being done, Your Honour, if I may make an inquiry. I'm a little confused as to what was the purpose of doing this sort of direct examination. Is it that the gentleman does not recall any of the events and this is sort of a past recollection recorded and therefore he is being refreshed or being presented with the opportunity to read often documents and therefore comment on them? Is it to just sort of bolster what's on the paper already that will obviously come in via the rules of evidence? I'm not quite sure whether this is testimony. What is the purpose of this? I think we should get a narration from Mr. Scott through the witness. He can ask open-ended questions, and I think if he needs to point to something to bolster the testimony, that may be fine, or for other purposes, but at this rate I'm not quite sure what it is that we're doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm happy to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Scott. The Defence is wondering what your purpose is by reading paragraphs. Do you wish to highlight the critical situation of Mostar, or what was the object of this manoeuvre?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Several answers to the question, Your Honour, and I'm happy that Mr. Karnavas has raised it because I think it does in fact raise an important issue and one that we've been discussing for some time. Number one, if does indeed indicate the contemporaneous record of the international observations of what was happening in Mostar during this time period. It may occur to the Chamber as time goes by in months ahead and if the Chamber reviews certain documents in the future. If the witness has said, as he has, that the Spanish Battalion was excluded from the Mostar area for a period of time how was it that they were reporting these observations? I thought the Chamber might want to know that in fact they were reporting -- they were receiving the information in the ways that the witness has indicated in the last few minutes, by radio, by other sources, by Muslim sources in Jablanica and elsewhere. It seems to me that this is information the Chamber might want to have. Thirdly, Your Honour, this illustrates exactly the point of the - - frankly the quandary or the difficult situation that the Chamber views about the admission of documentary evidence causes. If I do not show the witness the document, the Defence and perhaps the Judges will say at the end of the examination the document won't be admitted because it was never put to the witness. So I have to then take the witness through, according to these rulings, document by document by document. Now, I don't think that's the most efficient way to proceed, but if that's where we are, then I have no alternative.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may briefly respond, Your Honour. First of all, I don't see how this sort of line of questioning in the manner in which it's being done establishes some sort of contemporaneous record, that fact that Mr. Scott alluded to. Secondly, with respect to radio communications and what have you, how they were receiving the information, if we go back, the gentleman was shown a particular paragraph. Mr. Scott read it and then asked him a question about how were you getting your information. Now, he could have done this very simply. How were you receiving your information? Without showing him the document, of course. In other words, get a narration. I understand - now, the third point that Mr. Scott raises is rather interesting, because if I spend four days in just glancing through the documents and reading the critical ones and then I'm given by the Chamber 45 minutes to do cross-examination, here he is, he's complaining that he can't get his 3.000 documents in unless he does it in this fashion, and that poses the problem for us as well. And I think it might be more useful for perhaps the Prosecution to tailor its target, to figure out what it is they want to accomplish. What points are they trying to establish, and then perhaps introduce documents that establish those points or assist in establishing the points. But to throw at us, you know, thousands of documents is not helpful. Also, this is not an examination. I'm sorry. Reading a document and then asking him something that has nothing to do with the document is not exactly getting information from the gentleman. The gentleman is here to give us testimony. Let's ask, who, what, why, where why how and let him explain and then show a document for a particular point. I'm just trying to assist the Trial Chamber here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Scott, as the Defence has said, and I agree with him, you should be pursuing an objective. The paragraph that appeared on the screen was apparently used to describe the humanitarian situation in Mostar. Therefore, one should have asked the question -- one should have asked the witness the following question: Sir, could you describe the humanitarian situation in Mostar. Then he would have said there was no water, no medicine, et cetera, et cetera, then you would have shown him the document and said, Given everything you have said -- is everything supported by this document? And he would have said yes and then we would have moved on. Try to pursue your objective first and then present the relevant document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we can go on, sir, to Exhibit P 03705. While you're looking for that document, sir, if I can ask you, did you -- did the Spanish Battalion continue to make efforts during this time period, June, July, August, 1993, to gain access to Mostar or to block -- to break the blockade of the HVO to Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The SpaBat efforts were always aimed at doing precisely that, at being able to gain access to Eastern Mostar and to deliver humanitarian aid, because although we didn't know from reliable sources, we gathered the situation was critical, but we always came against the impossibility of getting the convoys through because of the HVO opposition.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you recall whether the Spanish Battalion officials, senior officers ever had occasion to have direct communications with HVO officers other than Mr. Bozic, such as General Petkovic, for example, or General Praljak, for the purposes of trying to gain access to Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Affirmative. Yes, we did try to establish contact with all the officers of the HVO, including the chief of our operations unit as well as other different chiefs of the headquarters. We tried to establish contact at all different levels including the officers in charge of the HVO who happened done in the area or with whom we had regular contact, Mr. Praljak, Mr. Bozic, Mr. Peskovic [as interpreted] and other officers of the headquarters of the HVO. I don't recall their names. It would be impossible after 14 years to recall all their names, but yes, we did try to establish contact with all of them through the headquarters. We tried to see them face-to-face. And the effort was to try and gain access into Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry, just to correct the transcript. On page 27, when you mentioned in Praljak, Mr. Bozic, Mr. Petkovic as compared to the transcript says Mr. Peskovic. Is it Mr. Petkovic, P-e-t?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall exactly the spelling of Mr. Petkovic. I'm not really sure, but now I can see it on the screen. I remember he was the officer in charge or the boss of the HVO, but I don't recall the act spelling of his surname.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Looking at exhibit P 03075, sir page 8 of the English version I believe it will be at stage 2 of the Spanish document.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you tell me what the date is that I can find it quicker?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes. It's the --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: More quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It's the 25th of July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me one moment. In the first -- well, there's a paragraphs that starts out it says "BH officials in Mostar." Toward the end of that paragraph it says "It is impossible for food and other essential items to reach this part of the town because of an HVO blockade of all access roads. According to these sources, there will soon be no food to feed so many people." Can you tell the Judges approximately how long this HVO blockade existed before you or the -- you being the Spanish Battalion or other international organisations were able to get access to Mostar, to the Muslim part of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to be able to ascertain the date and the duration in detail, but I would actually have to study in detail the logbook of operations because I cannot recall. But I think as I said it before in my statement it would have been for a period of between 20 and 30 days approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can next direct your attention, please, to Exhibit 39 -- 0398.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but I'm looking at the documents before me, certain subjects have already been addressed, but I can't fail to ask the following question: If you have a look at the document in front of you, have a look at the second paragraph. It says, "... Medjugorje." There are certain comments, observations concerning the vehicles circulating there. Could you read out the paragraph that starts with "Vehiculo blanco y verde," the white and green vehicle.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: "White and green police type-vehicle bearing the number plates HV/Croatian Army/687, two military trucks with lowered tarpaulins, no number plates were driving next to this vehicle. A completely white Nissan Petro, one of the models used by SpaBat bearing the plate HVO-880-M."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why does the document mention a vehicle with the registration number HVO 687? Why is it important?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe it was important because of the vehicles but particularly because they carry the number plates of the HVO and also because they were painted white and they could have been used as a UN vehicle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, we were about to go to Exhibit 3 -- 03980. If I could ask you to look at page 3 of the Spanish document and direct the courtroom's attention to page 5 of the English version. I'll point out one observation to you, and I have a question for you based on that. It is to -- it is dated the -- there is a number of dates on these documents. I want to give you the correct date if I can. 6th of August, 1993, your intrep number 255. And on page 3, I believe the Spanish version, if you can find -- it's a report again about what's happening in Mostar and there is this specifically, this specific passage if you can find it, please: "The food shortage and the increase in the number of refugees is making HVO operations against the Muslim zone easier." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dating to the 6th of August? No, I cannot find what you have just read.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Let me see if I can assist you. If you look in Exhibit -- it should be 3980.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. If you will go to I believe if you will look, please, at page 3 of the Spanish version of the document. A report concerning situation -- the condition and situation in Mostar. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: There is specifically the passage I read to you a moment ago and that is -- starts -- the sentence starts out "The food shortage." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, as a professional military soldier, can you assist the Judges with how a food shortage and an increase in the number of refugees in Mostar would make the HVO operations against the Muslim zone easier?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is -- that has been used throughout all wars to exert pressure on the civil population due to the look of food shortage and the - - an increased number of refugees. It makes it difficult for actions to be undertaken by one particular army and therefore facilitate, without a doubt, military action on the part of the HVO. So there is a siege. And what you try and do within a siege is to try and cut down means of transportation and food delivery to the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if I can next direct your attention to Exhibit P 04423, which is dated the 22nd of August, 1993, and should be your intrep 271. And, sir, if I could ask you to look, please, at page 3, page 3 in the Spanish version, page 5 in the English version. If you can find the following language, sir: "Under other information, heading capital, large capital A, "A convoy of the Canarias group entered the area of Mostar today. The people in the convoy were Mr. Thornberry, UNPROFOR civil affairs, Colonel Morales, et cetera." Do you see that passage?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, sir, this report is dated the 22 of August -- or 19 -- or 21st of August, 1993. If you can confirm that to yourself, please. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. That is the date of the intrep, the time of entry that was 21 August.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell the Judges whether it was this time toward the latter part of August, 1993, was the first time after substantial period of time that the international community was able to gain access to Mostar, actually enter the city of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, within the movement of this convoy. I know very well because I was part of it and I was in it. It was the first time after a long period of time that we were able to enter into Mostar and take humanitarian aid to that area of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, a bit more about how that convoy, if you can recall, how at that convoy was organised and anyone on the HVO side that you or your senior colleagues had dealings with to arrange this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within this convoy after a number of negotiations we arrived at the conclusion or at the decision, rather, to be able to take humanitarian aid both in the Muslim and Croat areas of Mostar, and we formed a convoy whereby we would take materials or supplies to both areas, a convoy, a two- branch, if you want, a convoy, I would take that convoy. I was in charge of both branches. And -- and that was -- that took a lot of work to be able to go into the eastern part of Mostar, because in the city of Cilu [as interpreted], which was an area that belonged to the Croat, the refugees were made to stop in front of the convoys and for a period of two or three hours were not able to continue, and thanks to the intervention of Mr. Praljak, of the then General Praljak, who then organised a passage of the convoy to the Muslim area. We were in the Muslim area that evening and that night, and it was that convoy that was also detained by the Muslims for a number of days, five days to be precise. There was the UNPROFOR, and we were detained in the eastern part of Mostar. And I don't know whether you need any further details or whether that should suffice.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Before we go on, on the name of the town. I don't have the transcript in front of me. You -- in the transcript we have Cilu on page 10 of line 32. The name of the town you referred to a moment ago where you said the convoy was stopped, was that in the village of Citluk?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Citluk. I do not recall the spelling exactly, but I think that as it appears on the screen now it should be correct, but I'm not certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I ask you please sir to look at -- this will be in the earlier bundle. It is the logbook which -- it may be quick enough it we can see -- if we can show the witness the Spanish version of P 01717. It's the logbook. And, sir, if I could direct your attention to the entry in the logbook the 26th of August, 1993, and for those using the English version, page 152.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, what date was that again? Did you say 29 or --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: 26th of August, 1993, I believe, sir. You look at the numbers on the document you're using, the numbers in the upper right-hand corner. You might find the number R016-7873, if that assists you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do have it in the logbook of operations dated 26th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry. Give me a moment to find ... I'm sorry. I may have the wrong reference. Sorry, Your Honour. I don't want to take the Court's time. Perhaps during the break I'll be able to find it. Somehow my point of reference seems to have gone missing, at least for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While you're looking for the document, one of the Judges would like to put a question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I'd just like you to clarify something else for us. You said that you had difficulties in front of the town of Mostar. You couldn't get in, and you often had to contact the HVO authorities, and they provide you with rather positive explanations but in fact it wasn't possible to enter the town. In front of the town of Citluk you contacted General Praljak, and the situation was resolved. Did you then continue to avail yourself of this possibility in order to accomplish your mission more easily? Did you contact people who had more influence in the field, the others who had higher positions like the vice Minister of Defence but in fact failed to obtain practical results in the field?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Frankly, in the statement I said that many of the movements were actually forbidden, but in the relation to this convoy movement, when we were trying to get into Mostar negotiations had already taken place, but with the HVO as well as BiH to come into the two areas, the Muslim and the Croat areas. And in relation to the refugees, there was no contact with the HVO. I correct myself. I use the word contact with the upper echelons, but we did not gain access. I personally did not come into contact with anybody, but despite after two hours, we saw the emergence of General Praljak and him made it possible for passage to be made available and for the convoy to continue to the eastern part of Mostar. And I remember that with the Croat minister who tried and yet this yielded no results, and when he ordered for passage to be given, no passage was achieved or obtained. So it was rather difficult period of time. We went through a very difficult time. Then because the population was very alarmed and they were trying to attack the vehicles, this was civilian population, and Mr. Praljak resolved this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To pursue this question which the Judges believe is very important, I'd like to ask you the following: Mr. Praljak, General Praljak, arrived at the site by chance as far as you can remember, or did he arrive there? Did he appear? Because that was the result of negotiations that had previously commenced.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand that -- that both the HVOs and the BiH had come to a decision to allow the convoys into both parts of Mostar. I think that they had committed themselves and they were going to see it through. But in terms of the refugees at Citluk, we established radio contact with our headquarters or upper echelons in Medjugorje, and I think it was them who established contact with the HQA of the HVO. And I understand that when the news was reached by the HVO headquarters, it was then General Praljak who took the initiative to attend in person to try and resolve this issue in situ. And I think that if one of the telephone calls made by our upper echelons to the upper echelons of the HVO, well, that made it possible to gain access.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Prior to this event, yourself or your collaborators or your bosses, did they contact General Praljak to resolve the problem of UNPROFOR movement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We had established contact with the HVO to facilitate the movement of that convoy. I do not recall. It wasn't my mission to establish the negotiation or to undertake the negotiations. I simply directed the operations of the convoys, and it was not me who established the contact. But I -- I think that there was contact made between the authorities and arrangements had been made for the convoy to enter the eastern area of Mostar, so that then humanitarian aid could be provided to both the Muslim and Croat areas of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you say there was contact with the HVO, that doesn't mean anything for the Judges. What we want to know is who, within the HVO, actually took the decisions? To say that there was contact with the HVO doesn't help us make headway. I believe I have understood you well when you said that you had contact, frequent contact, with the deputy minister of defence, but did you have any other form of contact at a higher level?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Spanish group had contact, maintained contact, never lost it, with the high command of the HVO. With whom did we speak in particular directly? Well, it depended on who initiated the negotiation. If it was somebody within the high command or the higher command of our group, it was then possible to establish a higher command with the local counterparts. But if it was the idea to try and establish contact with the higher authority, it would have been then the minister for defence or General Praljak or the minister of defence himself, Mr. Bruno Stojic. So we -- yes, we always went to the leader of the command wherever possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last question before we have the break. Was the liaison officer that your battalion had in the HVO headquarters, was there a liaison officer in the HVO headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it wasn't working exactly like that. It was not to amaze who had liaison officers within the high are commands. We would contact the high command of the HVO and would speak to one of the officer and we would tell them that we wanted to talk to the authority who was in a position to resolve the problem. As a general rule, it was the highest authority within the HVO or directly General Praljak or simply directly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Spanish Battalion did not have a liaison officer in the ABiH headquarters or in the HVO headquarters, and as a result when there was a problem you would make a phone call, and you would then reach some low-level officer. You wouldn't have direct contract with high-level officer since there were no liaison officers. If there had been a liaison officer, you would have contacted your liaison officer who would then have gone to the office of the HVO command -- to the office of the HVO command.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is affirmative. We tried to establish a liaison officer at the HVO, because after a number of days, this official or this liaison officer was not very effective or efficient, and we were not able to establish contact with the higher authorities. We had to then go to the highest-level authority, and this wasn't always possible because there were four people, whom I had mentioned before, who were not always there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You say he left because this didn't bear any fruit. Is that what you're saying, or your command ordered him to leave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Affirmative. In two normal -- our in cooperation, there is an exchange liaison officers, and it is through them or themselves that requests are made. In this particular case, the cooperation with the HVO had actually was not occurring any more, and whereby access to vehicles was not allowed. It was absurd to have a liaison officer in this area where this liaison officer had nothing to do. So there were times when he was placed there and there were other times where in particular at a particular time on at that date there was no contact, there was no liaison officer therefore, and the conversation was not fluent. Normally it would have been fluent and we would pick up the phone and we would say that our boss or our officer in charge wanted to establish communication with one of the HVO authorities. Normally it would have been the minister of defence, General Bozic, and we wanted to establish contact with him or any other one of their military officers in charge. The relationship was a rather fluid one. There was no problems of relationship with them. Whether they listen to us or not, there was a different issue altogether, but there was no problem in communicating with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, thank you. It's quarter to 4.00, so we're going to take the technical break and reconvene. I've just been told for technical reasons we'll have to make a half-hour break. So -- I don't know why, but we'll reconvene at 4.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, you have the floor. Counsel Nozica, you have a problem with the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. I do. The last part of the witness's sentence in response to the question when he was talking about communication with Mr. Bozic, he said, "But I did not have any problems in communicating with him," and that was recorded, and he added, "I don't know how far they listened to us," which was not recorded and which I consider to be important. We can, of course, ask the witness first whether he did indeed say that, and then I'd like to have that sentence added for the record. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I didn't quite get the question. What is the question? Did I say that? Is that the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you say that you had no problems communicating with Mr. Bozic, but that when you rang up, I don't know whom, you didn't know whether they listened to you. Is that what you said? That's how the Defence understood it. Is that what you meant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not exactly what I said. I said that we did not have any communication problems. We could speak with the Croatian authorities, and I wasn't referring to anybody in particular but to the high command officials, and then I said that they would not heed us. They would not heed us. They would not pay any attention to us. We could always speak to them, we could say, We want to go through such-and- such a checkpoint, but then they would not heed us. It was not that they would listen to us but they would not pay any attention to our request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you saying that they heard what you said but they didn't heed what you said? Is that right? Affirmativo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed, affirmative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Scott, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Witness BJ, in the few minutes before the break, there was a series of questions coming largely from the Judges in terms of what efforts the senior officers of the Spanish Battalion made to interact and have communications, in fact we were just talking about it again, with senior officials on the HVO side. Can I direct -- in this connection, can I direct your attention, please, to -- we were looking a moment ago at Exhibit P 01717, the logbook, and if you can please find the entry for the 15th of August, 1993. And for those in the courtroom using the English version, I believe it will be found on page 141. Sir, do you have the entry for the 15th of August, 1993? If you will look down several items --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apology. If you will look down, sir, several items until you get this language, "Talks were conducted it highest level to make it possible to repair the Bijeli bridge. To this end, a dinner was organized in the Medjugorge detachment, attended at the representatives of the HVO Mr. Prlic, Prime Minister, Mr. Stojic, Defence Minister." Do you recall, sir, whether you attended that dinner meeting with those two officials? Would it have been the normal custom for you to attend such a dinner function?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had I belonged to the detachment at the time, I would have attended that dinner because I would have attended that type of dinner, but I remember that precisely at that date I was absent. I was in Spain. I'm not altogether certain, but I do not remember having attended a dinner with Mr. Prlic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you recall the situation concerning the Bijela bridge and whatever problems that presented to UNPROFOR and the international organisations during this time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: See, yes, at -- the Bijela bridge, it was destroyed. We were trying to repair it so as to facilitate the transportation of convoys. There was a Slovene detachment, I think, repairing it. We put them up with the Spanish detachment. We carried out all kinds of studies in order to be able to carry out the repairs, but the HVO did not allow us to get anywhere near the bridge either to carry out the studies and much less the repair.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I ask you to go forward several days in your -- in the logbook to the 7th -- excuse me, to the 19th of August, 1993. For those using the English document, page 145. And in connection, sir, with the access to the city of Mostar, can I please direct your attention to this language: "A commission composed of Mr. Cedric Thornberry, deputy head of the civil affairs of the UN in the former Yugoslavia, Colonel Morales and the various representatives of the civil affairs and of the SpaBat command staff entered the city of Mostar today. They had a meeting with Croat officials in city, Mr. Bruno Stojic, HVO Defence Minister; Mr. Slobodan Bosic, HVO deputy Defence Minister; and Mr. Zeljko Toler HVO deputy commander. Can you tell us, sir, do you recall attending that meeting on the 19th of August, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No translation].

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I didn't get any translation.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not attend that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the role of Mr. Thornberry was at this particular time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: One thing I think I remember and it's stated here in the logbook, he was the second man in command of civil affairs at the United Nations. I can't remember who the first man was, but I think he was second. And he was with us in the convoy that got into Mostar. He was on that convoy with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And in that respect, sir, then if I could direct your attention forward finding the reference that I was looking for earlier today, if you'll look at the 21st of August, 1993. In the English document it's page 147. Do you see the references to "After long negotiations in the previous days, it was possible to enter the Muslim quarter in the city of Mostar. The group commander led the convoy. He was accompanied by Mr. Cedric Thornberry, international press, and members of the command staff." Now, sir, did I hear you correctly earlier today when you said you were also present in this convoy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Affirmative. I was in charge of that convoy, militarily speaking. Now, if the high chief of the Canarias group who was there, because Mr. Thornberry was present, would also be presents, obviously he would take in control, but I was in charge of that particular operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And continuing on, it says: "After crossing the lines of both sides and two mine obstacles in the area in the Mostar airport area, we managed to enter the Muslim area after almost two months of inability to do so." Now, sir, I've asked you about this time period several times day. Does that refresh your memory that there was an approximate two-month period until the end of August that the Muslim part of Mostar had been under blockade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Every single time you've asked me I'd actually didn't know because I didn't have the logbook in front of me and I didn't actually know the dates. But having seen the logbook now, perhaps not really two months, but 20 days, definitely, 20 days definitely during which Mostar was completely off-limits, East Mostar. You could sometimes get the impression that you were getting into Mostar but you were not actually getting into Mostar itself. This is why I previously made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you entered Mostar around the 21st of August, 1993, did you have occasion to see both East Mostar and West Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We got into both areas, east and west.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges briefly, please, your own observations as to the situation and conditions in East Mostar when you arrived on the 21st of August?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me correct something here that I have just seen now looking at the dates. Perhaps you are looking at a convoy of the 27th and now we're speaking about a convoy on the 21st. On the 21st when we got in, it was only for negotiation and it was only the Colonel, Mr. Thornberry and some vehicle. In that convoy I was no part of. I was speaking of another later convoy with humanitarian assistance where Mr. Thornberry was also present as well as Colonel Morales. On this particular one on the 21st of August I was absent and if I said earlier I was present, I now apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention, please, to the entry for the 26th of August, 1993. On page 152 of the English document. On the 26th of August, there is this entry about the fourth entry under that date: "The convoy that entered the Muslim quarter in the city of Mostar yesterday with a total of 19 trucks." Yesterday, by this log, being the 25th of August. Is that the date when the convoy actually entered Mostar, the 25th of August, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Affirmative. 25th of August at dawn, at dawn. It could already be the 26th of August, around 2.00 or 3.00 on the morning of the 26th of August because there was an exchange of corpses in the evening prior to that. So when we got into Mostar it would have been day break so that could have been 2.00, 3.00 in the morning of the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Going back to the question I put to you a few moments ago, can you tell the Judges, then, when you arrived on the 25th of August, 1993, what were the conditions or situation that you observed in East Mostar, the Muslim part of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the city was under siege. The most elementary things were lacking, were missing. In fact, our own food from our own armoured vehicle we gave out to the population. We emptied out our vehicle. We kept nothing for ourselves. People were really downcast, morale was very low. The entry of the convoy was like a boost to the morale of the population. This is what we noticed. But basically the most basic items were missing. We were shown part of the hospital, a lot of wounded. Many things were missing of all kinds for the whole of the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, I asked you a few moments ago, sir, did you also on that date or around that time also have occasion to go into West Mostar on the other side of the river, and I believe you said yes. Can you describe the condition and situation as you saw them on the west side of Mostar on the 25th of August?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on that particular date I did not go to the west side, I personally, but some of our convoys did go, and the overall impression was that on the other side of the river there was no need for humanitarian aid. There was a permeable, perfectly permeable border with Croatia, and there was nothing missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You've mentioned earlier today that when the -- after the convoy arrived in Mostar, the Muslim community did not want the convoy and UNPROFOR to leave, that they made efforts to detain the convoy. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Affirmative. The Muslim army placed civilians right in front of the armoured vehicles for us not to leave, but it was the Muslim army who directed them to stand in front of us. It wasn't the population of their own volition.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And do you recall the Muslims, either those representatives of the army, the ABiH, or members of the civilian population, telling you why it was they didn't want you, that is you being UNPROFOR, not to leave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the person who was telling us why they didn't want us to leave and they didn't let us out, in fact, was Isakmo [as interpreted] who was head of the Mostar Brigade if my memory doesn't fail me, a Muslim of that particular unit. He came up onto our armoured vehicle where the colonel and I were present, and he told the colonel, "Sir, you're being with -- detained here, and you will not be allowed to leave Mostar." In fact, his point was for the international community to know what conditions Mostar was under, and he felt that if we were kept in Mostar, that would put an end to any bombing or to any acts of aggression against the city of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In the entry that I just directed your attention to a few moments ago for the 26th of August, 1993, in the same paragraph do you see this language: "The BH officials claim they had detained the convoy because they were expecting an imminent attack by the HVO"? Do you recall something like that being said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Muslims gave all kinds of reasons. This is one of the reasons they gave, but basically what we all understood was that they wanted at least some sampling of the international community within Mostar so that they could bear witness of the bombing and the acts of aggression against the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. President, at this point, the Prosecution would propose to play some video material which I will get the exhibit number for you in a moment. Exhibit P 09676, which is a video that covers certain parts of the Spanish Battalion's tour in Mostar in the summer of 1993. We will be playing that in sanction.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, sir, if you will follow along the video. We may have -- there may be several questions either from me or from the Judges or later from the Defence concerning the video.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Last Tuesday, these images went around the world.
