After five days and six nights detained as hostages in the city of Mostar, kept as human shields by the Muslim militias and the civilian population of the city, 63 Spanish legionnaires managed to return to their headquarters in Medjugorje in Central Bosnia." "All started as a routine mission, in this meaningless war which is destroying the former Yugoslavia. Bosnia has turned into the most critical zone. The possibility of partitioning this country into three republics, Serbian, Croatian, and Muslim, has brought the three forces in conflict into a relentless ethnic cleansing with an aim to secure the possession of as much territory as possible. In this war, the Muslims, abandoned by Europe and the US, get the worst part of it, under an imposed general weaponry embargo which in practice only damages them. They were reduced to small part of territory of less than 30 per cent of the country in which they were majority and under terrible sieges: Sarajevo, Graz and Mostar." "In Mostar, which the Croats expect to turn into the capital of the self-proclaimed Republic of Herceg-Bosna, there is a Muslim ghetto with between 38.000 to 50.000 people. They're piled up without water, electricity, food, no medicine. Mostar is situated within the area of responsibility of the blue helmets of the Tactical Group Canarias, the Spanish contingent group, whose mission is to maintain open the corridor of humanitarian aid along the Neretva River, a peacekeeping operation for which the Spanish soldiers have paid a high price: Ten deaths and around 30 wounded." "Through the ministry of foreign affairs, measures are being taken in New York, at the United Nations, in Geneva, the seat of the peace conversations in Zagreb, and in other European capitals. On the other hand, our military representatives in the field have conducted direct negotiations with the local leaders, which resulted in our managing to complete our objective from the very beginning: A cease-fire. The aim was not to rescue the detained Spanish soldiers but to obtain a cease-fire that would protect the civilian population from the sufferings they had been experiencing for several months already." "In the area of Mostar, the escort of eight convoys is the responsibility of the Spanish blue helmets, but in Bosnia the convoys of humanitarian assistance sent to one of the parties in the conflict frequently bump into the ill-will of the adversaries. There had already passed two months without an ounce of humanitarian assistance succeeding to get through the Croat fence around Mostar, when Colonel Morales, chief of the Spanish blue helmets force, decided on the 21st of August to send a convoy with medicines to the Muslim sector Mostar." "The first convoy for Mostar went through safely. The Spanish legionnaires on board of their armoured vehicles delivered to the Muslim neighbourhood two tonnes of medicine taken from their own field hospital based in Medjugorje and were received with great joy by the population. The Spanish gave their own individual food rations to the women and children that besieged their vehicles." "The success of this first mission made Colonel Morales determined to organise a second convoy, this time with 300 tonnes of food to be transported with the United Nations trucks. After difficult negotiations, both with the Croat militias and the armija, the Bosnian Muslim army, the Spanish blue helmets contained an agreement to deliver the convoy to be followed by a cease-fire and an exchange of dead bodies between Bosnian and Croats. The convoy started on the wrong foot. The Croat population from Medjugorje and Citluk blocked the path denying the possibility for an assistance to be sent to the population of Mostar. This delayed the progress and it was not before the evening that the convoy reached the outskirts of Mostar. There, on an abandoned airstrip of the airport, the exchange of dead bodies from both sides, victims of the latest combats, took place. Meanwhile, the cease-fire was being observed, and the macabre exchange was done under the lights of vehicles. Thereafter, in the dark, the convoy proceeded to cross the confrontation lines and went into Mostar. When we finally arrived, I believe you can see the satisfaction reflected on my face because of the fact that we have arrived with a convoy of humanitarian aid to Mostar, although with many difficulties along the way, many negotiations and many stops, but I believe that it is rewarding and comforting to see all these people that have around us satisfied and happy because we have arrived to this side of Mostar." "The 300 tonnes of food were unloaded in three hours. Meanwhile along their armoured escort vehicles, the Spanish legionnaires awaited an order for departure. The cease-fire was kept, and the civilian population was friendly with the Spanish. Nevertheless, when, at 3.00 in the morning, an order was given to depart, the mood changed. The armed members of the armija started encircling the convoy obstructing their departure, fearing that immediately after the cease-fire ended the Croats would launch an attack. The armija placed women and children on the road obstructing the passage for the convoy and threatened that it would shoot at the convoy if they abandoned the city. 160 people, Spanish military and members of the UN, stayed as hostages in Mostar. Whether that was ordered by the armija or leaders of some other group which is also a possibility, I cannot say with certainty at this moment. I cannot confirm it at this time. But what we cannot do ever, neither the Spanish soldiers nor the United Nations, is that we cannot respond to these people in any violent form. We tried to negotiate and to make them understand that perhaps this is not the best way to continue receiving humanitarian aid, but we cannot put pressure on them either." "In the Spanish general headquarters in Medjugorje as well as Sarajevo and at other I national levels, five days of tense negotiations followed. Hopeless and mistrusting both the United Nations and a Europe that had abandoned them, left on their own, the Muslims from Mostar demanded part of the Spanish blue helmets to stay indefinitely there to prevent future Croat attacks, disobeying even the orders from their own government in Sarajevo. On the other hand, Colonel Morales, a hard and experienced man, refused to make any kind of concessions until the totality of his men were safely out of Mostar. Only for security reasons he allowed, after a couple of days, the exit of civilian personnel that were part of the convoy, but he and his military men stayed on the main street in the city under an intolerable heat, without water, insufficient food during five days. Five days of tension that did not prevent the Spanish legionnaires from continuing helping the civilian population as was the case of saving a wounded man on a street under sniper fire." "Finally, on Tuesday the 31st, Muslims from Mostar permitted the convoy to exit the town pursuant to a general agreement with included an extension of the cease-fire in the city. Mr. Javier Solana, minister of foreign affairs. 'Spanish soldiers fulfilled their obligation which was fundamentally to provide humanitarian assistance and avoid the situation of danger. I believe that we must first say that the conduct of the Spanish soldiers was magnificent and was recognised by the whole world. Spanish soldiers did not want to leave Mostar without getting a cease-fire agreement first. We were working together with the UN and with both parties to obtain the cease-fire agreement so that the Spanish soldiers could leave Mostar only when the main goal of the mission had been accomplished and this was the delivery of humanitarian assistance. Together with their colonel, the 62 Spanish soldiers and 12 armoured vehicles crossed the confrontation line and travelled the 30 kilometres to Medjugorje and then and only then did Spanish patrols start to go into the Muslim and Croat sectors of Mostar in order to monitor the cease-fire. "Finally the blue helmets arrived to the headquarters in Medjugorje." "The left, Muslim side, for Muslims and all those who believe in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Spanish Battalion is the last hope, a final link before withdrawal and perishment. In the same way that Sarajevo is a symbol for Bosnia, Mostar is a symbol for Herzegovina, the symbol of multi- ethnic community, Serbs, Croats, Muslim, Jewish tradesmen under Ottoman Empire, the destruction which was first caused by Serbs last year when they were driven out by Muslims and Croats has grown 10 times larger since May 9th. Nowadays, Croats want their part of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Serbs too. Their argument is clear: The Croatian state is where Croats live. Blue helmets, it's pretty but they are destroying it. When people are killing each other. I mean, the fighting against a country and then the fighting amongst each other, but well, let them do what they want to." "This is destroyed. There's nothing to do here. Well, we're trying to prevent them from hitting each other but they still do it." "Well, we don't know how long we'll be staying. We came here for 24-hour guard duty but that could be extended because it could happen later on that the control in charge of letting us pass through never arrives. We always come here with at least three days' worth of rations, and as I already said, the situation is difficult." "Didn't you receive special instructions precisely because there is a possibility that you might find yourselves under specific situations? "Well, we don't know why we arrived here and initially in principle we must not respond to fire unless it be straight directly -- directed straight to us. Rifle fire within these armoured vehicle is no problem because it's well prepared to stop it. But of course a mortar shell or a grenade, yes, that can hurt. And we see anyone aiming a mortar at us, then of course we'd have to open fire." "As Spanish troops testify daily, tragedies are lining up one after another in the face of the realistic general state of indifference. Like in Mostar where ethnic cleansing is still being carried out, the Croats are intimidating, expelling and gaoling Muslims with the aim of transform the town into a purely Croat town. This man says how he was expelled last year by the Serbs. He lost a son last year. He still has one other son and another daughter and he thanks God because things could still be worse, he says, or this Bosnian soldier who is fighting for a state which everybody things is already dead. With some 30 or so bullets per soldier, they are facing a much more numerous force, well-equipped, and in solid artillery positions, which is holding them in sight from the heights just like the Serbs held them in Sarajevo." "We will resist till the end he says. We no longer believe in peace nor in the Croats and we say to them that we will fight to the last man. We have nothing to lose." "To isolate them even more, Croats from the HVO, a paramilitary organisation, the Croatian Defence Council, trained and supported by Zagreb, are trying unsuccessfully to blow up this bridge reconstructed with humanitarian aid from the US. Due to an escalation in conflict along the Neretva River in Herzegovina, in the zone in -- in the zone which is under their control, in order to support them in their difficult task people who are spending entire days in their armoured vehicles without the possibility of coming out are enduring marathon shifts, 200 new soldiers, 70 logistics personnel and 120 legionnaires have arrived as reinforcements. "Since a massive house to house arrests of Muslims by Croats from the early dawn which began last may 9 most of whom are still held in the Heliodrom in Mostar, the position of the Spanish blue helmets in the area is delicate. We're currently trying to solve what we can to mediate and to try to avoid further shooting, but mostly we are dealing with the civilian population and refugees whom we are rescuing to ensure that people are no longer taken prisoner and to avoid houses being vacated." "Whilst trying to negotiate in order to maintain some sort of stable or unstable status quo, hatred erupts amongst both sides." "It was useless for international mediators to meet again with representatives of both sides. In the high-level meetings under the auspices of the Spanish Battalion, the Bosnian and Croatian representatives attended. However, this only underlined the tremendous disagreement existing amongst the parties." "The day after the meeting in Siroki Brijeg, Franjo Tudjman--"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we perhaps stop this, because Mr. Praljak has, in fact, stood up. Mr. Praljak, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We should have the dates put in order here, because all the years and months are confused in this film. We need some order, chronological order in order to be able to follow what is happening. This is a collage of various excerpts and covers a period over one year. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps the questions that will be put after we've seen the video will clarify anything that is not quite certain. Can we continue now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] The powerful lobby from the region had paid for his campaign and was now requesting that it be an integral part of Croatia." "In the field tents, the Bosnian military leader Mr. Halilovic, Mr. Petkovic, the Croatian one often discussed in the presence of the Spanish colonel Mr. Antonio Morales. 'A month ago I begged you on my knees that you helped us to rescue people from the mountain both Muslims and Croats but you negotiated with the Serbs you didn't realise that they wanted to finish with us first and then to finish with you as well.'" "Colonel Morales: In about an hour, an hour and a half, these two sides which are situated in the region and that are EC observers and the members of the Canarias Tactical Group will see what is going on in the field in order to inform the mixed committees about it. There was only one opportunity to take both sides to see the devastated areas in the region. A few kilometres from the base, both sides looking at each other with mistrust and preparing for what may follow. The Croats have tanks, mortars people who alive along the road they control. The Muslims who have taken up positions, rarely get weapons, and when it does happen they hurry to learn how to handle them in groups. The greatest strength on the other side both in the town and on the mountain lies in that they are going for all or nothing. The main task of the Spanish blue helmets is to reduce tensions between the Croats and the Muslims even though they have already suffered some casualties because of this." "Lieutenant Colonel Alonso: In the remaining part of the road towards Tarcin, we have an area of conflicts in Konjic. There's a group of snipers that pound the road and do not allow the movement of vehicles, mainly civilian vehicles. They have not fired at us yet, but we have already detected certainly firing at civilian vehicles using that road in both directions." "From their positions on hills on the western part of Mostar, the HVO forces started at dawn the savage attack on the left bank of the Neretva River, the heart of the capital of Herzegovina populated by Bosnians. Their initial targets, Titov bridge and the headquarters of the 4th Corps of the BiH army, are located in a civilian building. Like in the worst case of the most savage dictatorships, the prisoners, the majority of them civilians, are taken to a football stadium. The Croats have made civilian prisoners by arresting them in their own homes. Prisoners have been taken in the direction of Citluk and they will be confined in the Tito's army former helicopter pilot's headquarters in Rodoc. In total, it is estimated that the fate of 400 people is unknown. The propaganda from the HVO keeps releasing false communiques according to which their operations of putting Muslims in prisons are only preventive operations. They claim that this region belongs to them since the 13th century."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Witness BJ, you have watched this video material that has been...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Witness BJ, you have just watched this video material being presented in the courtroom. Can you tell the Judges, please, what you saw in this video, does that give a fair presentation, a picture of what you saw and experienced in Bosnia in 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honours. Your Honours. Excuse me, sir. Going back to Mr. Praljak's objection. We don't have a foundation for this film. We don't know what period it covers. As was indicated, it is a montage, and now it seems that we're using footage from God knows where just to sort of ask general questions. I don't think it's proper. I know that in this Tribunal, anything goes as far as bringing in evidence. I mean, anything, but this is beyond the pale as far as showing something and then saying, Well, does this comport with what you saw happening. You know, so it goes along the same lines as someone's feelings, you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, shortly before the end of this video they mentioned the beating of the Muslim part of Mostar or the shelling of the Muslim part of -- of Mostar, and the video quite clearly demonstrated that it was the other part of Mostar that was being shelled. So it's an error, and there are many such errors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Scott, the first problem is the problem that concerns the dates. The video contains various elements that the witness could certainly put a date to. There were his colleagues, Colonel Alonso and others, who held meetings. Perhaps on that basis one could arrive at precise dates. They could put things back into a framework.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I will be happy --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I will be happy to ask additional questions, Your Honour. As explained, the Court may remember back to when Mr. -- when Witness BJ was here before and the efforts to obtain this video footage, and as we've explained to the Defence in several letters since we obtained it some weeks ago, this came from a Spanish television station in Spain which obtained much of the footage from the Spanish Battalion, which is the footage that Witness BJ referred to when he was here in June. Now, I will -- let me first of all, sir, ask you the general question that I asked you and then I'll go back and take you there some additional specific questions. And my general question to you, sir, is what you saw this afternoon in the few minutes of video material that were displayed, is that -- does that present a fair portrayal of your experiences and observations during your tour of duty in the Mostar region in 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me interpose the same objection. It obviously calls for speculation on the part of the witness, and to make a general question of that kind when we had so many different episodes portrayed in the -- in the video, there being no foundation that this witness was present on most of those occasions, Your Honour, it's not an acceptable question. It calls for speculation, and as Mr. Karnavas said, even by the lax rules of evidence here, it's not an admissible way to proceed. So I make that objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, many things have been said in the last two minutes are just flat wrong. Perhaps the counsel does remember the previous testimony of this witness either in June or today. The witness clearly gave testimony in June about footage being taken on the 9th and 10th of May, 1993, which showed people being gathered on the football pitch, which showed people being taken, led -- men being led to Mostar. He testified about that in June, and that was covered in the film. He has also testified or would testify about the meetings, some international meetings that took place in the Mostar region around the 18th of May. He's also talked about the arrival of the convoy on approximately the 21st, excuse me, or that is the 25th of August. He spoke about that. He spoke about how the UNPROFOR people were kept in Mostar by the population. That was shown on the video. Your Honour, the witness has discussed virtually everything that was on the video, gave testimony as to everything that was on the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. If I may intervene. It appears to us that the Chamber is able to relate what the witness has already said to what the Chamber has been shown, which is not entirely different from other image material that we have also been shown. I wonder whether the witness could not be asked whether there were any images of events in this video in which he attended and what his specific memory of the specific event is. I must confess that the appreciation of the film is not facilitated by the fact that it practically ends with the beginning, because what we see in the very end is the shelling of the headquarters. That was the very start of it all, and so one -- I must confess that it is somewhat confusing. It's a nice illustration, but to what extent it is really useful as evidence, I think, is in fact open to doubt. I must confess that I am not unimpressed by the objection of the Defence. So perhaps if you could turn around and go to specific experiences of the witness rather than general impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I could add something to what Judge Trechsel has said -- just said. Could the Prosecution ask the witness to distinguish between the images that he was an eyewitness of. He participated in certain events, and could he then distinguish such events from events that he didn't participate in. Then we're just speaking about hearsay. This TV footage covers a period of number of months, and as the Defence has said, the footage has been put together. Mr. Praljak mentioned an important problem. There was an HVO shelling apparently, but the headquarters wasn't the right one. So there's an entire series of questions that one has to ask oneself. So please proceed in a concise manner so we can avoid the Defence getting up to raise objections, because this results in wasting time. Please move on progressively on the basis of what you are certain of and taking into account things that you are less certain of. In order to save time, I'll put a question to the witness. Sir, you have just seen a video, and could you tell us whether there were any events that were depicted in this video that you were present at?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In very many of the images I was present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Scott, please proceed and do your work. I'm not going to do the Prosecution's for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I've been trying to do for some minutes now. Let me just indicate before I continue with the witness. The video was received from the Spanish television station. The OTP did not seek to edit if any sort of way. We presented it the way it was presented to us. If it was not nicely done, I regret that. It was presented by the Spanish television station. Obviously, the Prosecution has not had the ability to meet with the witness since obtaining this because, as you know, the witness has sequestered from the Prosecution in the meantime so I've only had a chance to play it for the witness in the courtroom without having reviewed it with the witness previously at all. So we are operating at some disadvantage.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, having said, sir, you just indicated that there were certain parts of this video, events depicted in the video, that you were personally involved in or present. Can you identify and perhaps we'll talk about some of them in more detail but can you identify by identifying for us the parts of the video in which you were directly involved?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there's been two films here, two video films. In the second -- well, the second one is, in fact, covers the first two months or one and a half months of the time my grouping was there in Bosnia, and the second film is a film which basically talks about how the convoy was detained in Mostar. This is what I saw. As for the detention of the convoy while I was there, and I was present throughout the period, throughout the period covered by the film. So I have first-hand knowledge of what happened then with the convoy. I was involved in the negotiations. In the first part which corresponds to the second part of the film where there's a mixture there of images which may have come from television files or archives. There's a fundamental reason for this perhaps. The journalist who interviews in the first month Angela Rodicio [phoen], was there. She was the one who filmed that. And in the send part there was a different journalist who was present during the convoy's detention in Mostar. There are old images also involved, such as attacks on Croats or Muslims, bombings of Mostar, which I don't believe belong to the dates in which I was there, but I have to see the film again to confirm this. You saw also the transferral of Muslims by Croats something that happened in June, that I'd seen already and that was filmed by the Spanish Battalion, by units of the Spanish Battalion, and is shown at the beginning and at the end of the films. You see us going down the hill led by Croats. You see negotiations by Mr. Halilovic and Petkovic in Jablanica, and I was involved directly as a witness. I was not involved in negotiating itself. And you saw them within a tent. This is what we did. We provided a premises for them to negotiate. I was also involved in the tour undertaken by Colonel Morales and Petkovic in the northern part of Jablanica. That also was seen on the film. And I also participated, although I was not present when attempts were made to stop fighting against -- to stop fighting between HVOs and Muslims. So in the film itself you might see me a couple of times. Well, my back actually because I'm not very keen on being filmed but you can see me on the film itself on a couple of occasions. Now, if there's anything more specific I could perhaps be more specific or I clear up whatever you want me to clear up.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness be asked to slow down for the sake of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you hear that, sir? You've been asked to slow down a bit for the translation. All right. Sir, based on your answer just now let me go back and take you through some parts that you've told us. Accepting for the moment that the order of the video material might have been presented differently, did you see, in the video that was presented this afternoon, images that correspond to what you understood happened on approximately the 9th and 10th of May in connection with the attack on Mostar and the arrest, the taking of people to a football pitch and to the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. The question is whether he understood --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The question is whether he understood what happened. I guess perhaps it should be asked of what he saw, not what he understood. In other words, what he was told. So did he witness what happened on those dates and, if so, then the question can be does it correspond with as opposed to whether he understood something that was told to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't accept that, Your Honour. The Court --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- well knows that hearsay is fully acceptable in evidence here. It's not necessary that this witness personally heard it or saw it. Hearsay is admitted in this Tribunal every day, and has for the last 12 or 13 years. I don't accept Mr. Karnavas's position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: First of all, let's step back --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Counsel Karnavas, we've understood the point, and let me assure you that I will have to guide the witness's testimony and I'm going to go to the heart of the matter. You said that the Spanish Battalion filmed the presence of the citizens of Mostar at Heliodrom and their departure afterwards. That's what you've said. You've told us that. So we saw the footage, and we did see people on the stadium and people marching, the Velez stadium, and people on the move. Now, when this was asserted, were you there yourself? Did you see it for yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, negative. This was filmed by special units belonging to us, and we saw the film that was shot that very morning, but I wasn't present there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. Thank you. When you say "special units," does that mean filming crew or secret agents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Within our group, a unit of special operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You have said that you have seen these videotapes the same day.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I refer exclusively to the images taken by the Spanish Battalion which was the transfer of the Muslims who had been detained along the way and also at the Heliodrom. These images were shot by the Spanish Battalion unit and I was talking how we saw that on the very same day or the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: But that is an exception. Other parts of the film you have never seen before or have you seen some of it before or for the first time today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Many of these images I had already seen them on TV when I saw the interviews or the TV programmes, but not like they had been seen here in a continuous mode.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're telling us that special units filmed the presence of people at Velez stadium, the inhabitants, and then when they were on the move. That was also filmed by these special units. And you, yourself, in the battalion, you saw those images the same day; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please continue, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Witness BJ, I think we've covered the portion on the 9th and 10th of May. Did you also see in the tape meetings attended by such people as Mr. Izetbegovic, Franjo Tudjman, Lord Owen, Mate Boban and others? Did you see them in a meeting room around a series of tables? Did you see that portion of the tape?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Affirmative. I was there present at that meeting. I was one of the people in that meeting. I was a spectator at a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, that on approximately the 18th of May following the events of the 9th and 10th of May, that these series of meetings took place in the Mostar area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around that time I do not recall the dates exactly. Of course I would have to check the documentation, but yes indeed there were a number of meetings, and many attempts at a cease-fire, many cease-fires that had already been signed upon, had been agreed upon and which we thought we had overcome and nothing had been overcome. And there were other meetings, but if I had to refer to them, I had to look at them in detail. This one that was part of the video image, yes, I was present at those two meetings, but I would not like to refer to these meetings on a general basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could I ask you, sir, to look in Exhibit P 01717 for the date -- for the entry of the 18th of May, 1993. And for the users of the English document in the courtroom refer them, please, to page 65. If you can find the 18th of May, sir. The second entry for that day, sir, the second entry for that day, do you see reference to a meeting at the highest level attended among others by Alija Izetbegovic, Franjo Tudjman, Lord Owen, Mr. Thebault, General Wahlgren, Mate Boban, Petkovic, Halilovic? Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Affirmative. Yes, I can see that, that there was the meeting that was actually shown on the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, in your -- in the video we also saw -- excuse me. You made reference a moment ago when you said what you saw to meetings that took place in the Jablanica area. Can you tell us a bit more about that part of the video? When, approximately, do you recall those meetings occurring?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were perhaps two or three other meetings or two or three day, rather, during which the military chiefs met, and I was present at one of them during which a tour was organised in which I participated with General Petkovic on General Morales to see the northern area. We were present in the detachment of Jablanica, and we made all the needs available to them and to allow them to engage in meetings and negotiations, and that was also seen in the video. You see one of the officials who is standing up. He is not participating directly in the negotiations. But we were there. We just made the space available to them. I remember that there were possibly three meetings, but of course there were a lower number of meetings but at least two, if I could say, of that order, of that level of meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And finally, sir, a large portion of the presentation was concerned -- excuse me, concerned the arrival of the humanitarian convoy in Mostar. Is that the convoy that arrived, sir, on approximately the 25th of August, 1993, and then was detained there for a number of days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, what you see in the video are two. One arrived on the 21st of August which we referred to previously, and personally -- you see in this Colonel Morales in the armoured vehicle and in the other one, a larger convoy with Belgian trucks, and that entered on the 26th or 27th of August in that area, and that is also seen in the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And again, sir, were you personally involved in those events, the arrival and the convoy on the 25th of August and the days thereafter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the first one I did not participate personally. I participated in the organisation ,and the escort of that convoy. On the second opportunity, yes, I did. And in fact, you see my face in the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: don't say anything more to identify yourself, please, but I think we can leave it at that. Mr. President, I intend to move forward off the video material unless the Judges have additional questions at this time or -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Scott, I'm looking at the clock. How much more time do you need to complete the examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm afraid Your Honour, it will require the rest of today's session at the pace we've been able to go, which has been quite slow, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Registrar, could we have the calculations, please? But anyway, we have until quarter to six, which means 20 more minutes before the break, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall whether the Spanish Battalion during its -- and the Canarias group in particular, during its tour from approximately April 19th to approximately the 30th of September, 1993, did it make entries in its reports and log books about the evictions and transfers of Muslims from Mostar and other parts of Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand the question, whether I know of any transfers and detentions of Muslims in the area of Mostar. Could you repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes. That wasn't exactly my question. Do you recall when the Spanish Battalion made entries in and gave reports about these things happening in its reports and logbooks during this period? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps if I were to look into the logbook of operations, but I think that those entries have been included.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, as an example, sir, can I ask you to look at Exhibit P 03744, which is not the logbook but it is the intrep or it would be -- yes, the intrep number 246, for the 27th of July, 1993. Do you have that? And again, it's Exhibit P 03744.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps if you could show it on the screen I'll be able to see it as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Okay. If we could have the assistance of the usher then. If you can pull it up in the Spanish version, please. I believe it's on page 3 of the Spanish document, and approximately page 9 of the English document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Under the heading of "Miscellaneous," sir. If you can find number 5, miscellaneous. And under that, item number 2. It says: "An HVO police car which had its rotating lights on was seen in Vitina on the Grude-Ljubuski road. It was followed by three buses and 15 trucks carrying a large number of civilians, women, children, and the elderly, some of whom were seated and some were standing. An HVO military police van with five uniformed and armed individuals was at the tail end of the convoy. All the vehicles were drivable by uniformed military personnel. No luggage or parcels were seen on the vehicles. The civilians looked like country people. They appeared dispirited and some women were crying." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed. I see these here on the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you recall, sir, in your -- you said last time you were here there was -- there was a daily meeting, like a command staff meeting. Remember - do you ever remember things like that being discussed or reported in the daily reports that you also described the last time you were here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed. These information, even though this was covered during the briefing session, was convoyed to the operations unit and of course this information was known to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall any efforts that the senior officers of the Canarias group at this time, was any effort made to raise, to lodge protests or complaints with the HVO when observations, things like that were seen or observed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that every time that news were heard of events such as these occurring that conversations were maintained with the HVOs, and we asked them what were, the reasons behind these type of things, and we tried to establish or ascertain the movement of personnel or civilians, et cetera. And always the general response was that they were being displaced for security reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Try and speak slower, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, and also Mr. BJ, please kindly understand that you need the time for translation, and also you have to wait until the translation is being in a way done after each question and answer. Thank you very much indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Witness BJ, I think had you finished your answer, you finished before the Judges' quite proper intervention, and you said, "And always the general response was that they were being displaced for security reasons." Had you completed your answer? Was there any other further answer you want to make?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They -- it was always the general case that they provided that as an excuse, and it was always to do with security reasons, and that -- that was the reason why they were displacing the people, for security reasons, and that's -- that was how I concluded my statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You say that the HVO gave you the answer that this was for security reasons. Now, I thought I understood that you had special units. Now, these convoys escorted by the military police, they were going somewhere, weren't they? Couldn't you tell the responsible people in the HVO that such-and-such a convoy would be in such-and-such a place on a particular day at a particular time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Normally this type of information would almost always be obtained on a casual basis, and if one of our officers would observe something like that, would report this to us. And it wasn't that we were following the HVO officers or were undertaking intelligence work, because they were banned from doing this type of work. But every time there were patrols within the area, at times they would observe situations such as this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, to assume that it would not have been in accordance with your mandate if you had, for instance, surveyed such transport, followed them, seen what happened to those persons? That was not your task, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed. It was not allowed for us to undertake intelligence work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But you did so nonetheless.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course. What I make in -- and operations and undertaking some sort of intelligence work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, following on with your questions --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apology.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Following on with the questions put to you by the Judges, you've said in fact you did have conversations with the HVO, with HVO officers, and that the reason given was that these were -- or this displacement was for security reasons. Did you ever -- did you or General Morales or any of the senior Spanish Battalion staff receive satisfaction that this would be stopped or did you see it being stopped after you complained and protested about it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was always the same type of warning or the same type of notification given to the HVO. And in concrete terms in the film that we have seen here and the moment they -- they became aware of its existence, we told them that this will have serious consequences for you the moment the international community becomes aware of these types of events.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you told us the last time that you were here about the death of Lieutenant Castellanos who was hit by, I think, mortar fire on the 11th, about the 11th of May, 1993. Was that the only time in the tour of the Canarias group that a Spanish soldier, Spanish officer was killed or died in the course of the peacekeeping duties there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the time or the months in which the Canarias group was there, I think we had like 10 deaths and some over 30 people who were injured, and three people died when an armoured vehicle fell into the river. One lieutenant died being shot by a sniper. A lieutenant died as a result of a mortar being launched, and two others -- well, it could be said that it was as a result of suicide. Another one through a mortar grenade in Jablanica. One of them was being a sentinel at the detachment and when he was hit at the time. He was is sentry at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you be shown Exhibit P 04995. P 04995, which is an intelligence report, intelligence report number 294, 13th of September, 1993. And direct your attention to page 2 of the Spanish version. And directing others to page 5 of the English document. Under the heading marked -- it's 1.2, areas, and the first heading under that is Mostar, and then shelling. And do you see the section that talks about: "Today, 60 artillery/mortar grenades have fallen in the area of the main road of the Muslim quarter"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, sir, if we look through virtually your daily reports, these reports that were made on a daily basis, is that the kind of information that was routinely entered in your reports and logs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Affirmative. After the detention of the convoy, the -- the mission was to inform on this type of shelling, and the launching of projectiles in the Muslim area of Mostar. There was another section included in the report but almost always the shelling took place in the eastern part of Mostar, and therefore they were reported on regular basis in all the intelligence reports and in all reports dealt with the shelling of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me next -- let me take you to the next exhibit which is 0 -- I'm sorry. My apology. 04698. 04698, which is the report dated -- sorry. This is the part of the end-of-tour report, I believe, that we talked about last time, which we did replace it with the full version that was provided to us, which has been disclosed to everyone. Could I have the assistance the usher to provide the witness with a hard copy of the complete document. For the record, Your Honour, full versions of that document have also been provided to the Chamber. They were previously provided to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, again, if I could direct your attention, then, it's the part of the report concerning the area of Mostar. It is on -- hold on, Your Honour. We're pulling up the ... Sir, if you can find in your report where it talks about the -- it's the Tactical Group Canarias part of the report, the area of Mostar. It talks about the events on the 9th and 10th of May. If you find that. Do you have that, sir? And if you go down --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. And if you continue down several paragraphs you'll find a paragraph that says: "In consequence of the agreement signed by General Halilovic and General Petkovic, SpaBat units returned to the city." Do you see that? Okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And then skipping a couple of language, you'll see this sentence which is what I want to ask you about: "In the confrontation in the city, one of the parties to the conflict to wit the HVO is not very happy with the UNPROFOR presence in the city, direct and deliberate sniper attacks (boulevard) on SpaBat vehicles are therefore starting." Now, can you tell the Judges a bit more about the -- what you experienced and what the Spanish Battalion experienced in terms of as what's described here as "direct and deliberate sniper attacks"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Whenever SpaBat moved around the area of Mostar they came under sniper fire. Now, this sniper fire obviously could not hurt us within our armoured vehicles. Nonetheless, there was a lot of it. And there was even an anti-tank missile that was aimed at one of our cars, and that did considerable damage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, when we come to cross-examine this witness tomorrow, for example, about the 60 grenades, and when he's asked about Operation Neretva-93, the witness will state that he wasn't there at the time, and then what? What are we going to do then? Or, for example, the convoys being mentioned now in which a high-ranking HVO officer was, whereas the gentleman was in Spain. So how are we going to deal with that problem and resolve it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, why not wait until tomorrow rather than interrupting the examination-in-chief? You can say what you want tomorrow. But anyway, it's a quarter to 6.00. We've already been working for an hour and a half. So we're going to take a break and reconvene at 5 minutes past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Witness BJ, some of those making a record in the courtroom have asked me to ask for your assistance. Early this afternoon you made reference to the name of someone you described as the Mostar Brigade commander. For those who might wish to follow, it was at page 46, line 4, and what's written in the transcript now seems to be something along the lines of "Isakmo." I don't know can you possibly give us any other assistance of the name of the Mostar Brigade commander that you referred to earlier this afternoon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The last name of that person is Humo, H-u-m-o.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, we're going to have to try to move fairly quickly to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If you plan to move, I have a question. The last events that you have referred to, Witness, was you said that you were shot at by snipers and even by anti-tank guns. Have you complained of this to the HVO? To whom have you complained? What was the reaction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Whenever we were shot at, we complained to whoever we thought was firing at us. The problem is that very often that kind of fire was -- was right on the confrontation line, on the front line, and both sides said that the other side was responsible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On one of those particular incidents, sir, let me direct your attention to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention to the 11th of June, 1993. Did you have an officer by the name of Lieutenant Aguilar killed by a sniper on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges briefly because as I said our time is limited now because we'd like to finish your direct examination today, what happened concerning the shooting of Mr. Aguilar, Lieutenant Aguilar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you want Aguilar's section was giving humanitarian assistance to the Muslim hospital in Mostar. An agreement had been reached with the HVO to allow free passage to such medical assistance as long as there was a television crew filming it. And in fact, we had our own cameraman from the Spanish army, because we couldn't get hold of any press people at the time. We moved towards Mostar, and when we crossed the Tito Bridge, normally in that area the armoured vehicles were close and the Spanish soldiers got into the vehicles because this is when you came under fire, as I said earlier. However, in this -- in the instant case, Lieutenant Aguilar, in fact the only thing he did was to take shelter but without actually getting into the vehicle and closing it down. And unfortunately, as he -- as his armoured vehicle was crossing the Tito Bridge he was shot by sniper fire, crushed his spinal cord. He died immediately. We tried to react to that fire but we didn't know exactly where it had come from. Thereafter, there was an inquiry. The HVO authorities did take part in this inquiry into the death of Lieutenant Aguilar. We spotted the exact place from which the fire was shot -- from which that particular shot was fired, rather, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you describe to the Judges the location from which the shot was fired that killed Lieutenant Aguilar according to the inquiry?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was a building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Listening to the French interpretation, it was not the same like what we see on the transcript, because in the English text it is said that, "We spotted the exact place from which the fire was shot," and then, "From which that particular shot was fired, rather, and that's it." I believe it is not -- it doesn't reflect what probably our witness, BJ, said. So I wonder if you may repeat that particular paragraph which is -- which was your last part of your statement about Lieutenant Aguilar's death, which In English starts, "Thereafter, there was an inquiry." I wonder if you may repeat it for our benefit. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. What I said -- I'll repeat it. I'll repeat it. We located the area from which that shot was fired, and there was an investigation carried out by UN police, the Spanish authorities, the HVO, Croat authorities also cooperated throughout the investigation. They actually made it easy for us to carry out that investigation into the death of Lieutenant Aguilar, and we actually were able to spot the exact place from which that shot was fired. We took a picture of the building from which we believe that fire -- that shot was fired that killed Lieutenant Aguilar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You who were at the site, would you say that it's possible that an individual out of control might open fire on an UNPROFOR member? Is this, technically speaking, a possibility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Technically, of course. A sniper is always alone. He's never under the orders of anyone, and he can fire any time if he's got a target in view. Whether it was that sniper's own decision or a decision taken by the Croatian authorities is something I will not say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But did your investigation make it possible for you to identify the unit he was a part of or did it make it possible for you to identify a paramilitary group, or do you know nothing about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The sniper himself was not identified, but the place from which he was shooting. It was a sniper post definitely, and we saw exactly the trajectory of the bullet, and so therefore we know -- we believe, to the tune of 90 per cent, we know exactly where that shot originated.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Are you able this afternoon, sir, to describe that location for us, the building or location from which this shot was fired? If you can give us a physical description of the building as best you can recall.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, we're not getting any English translation, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Apologies from the English interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. The building that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please repeat your answer because it was not working in the B/C/S and English booth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The building opposite the Tito Bridge some 500 to 600 metres away. The distance then from the sniper to where the lieutenant was some 700 to 800 metres. It was the top of the building, the attic, a sort of -- it was a sort of makeshift building on the top of the building. The sniper had a very clear view of the whole Tito Bridge area and the Muslim region entry. If I could see plans of the area I could pinpoint the exact location.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask that the witness please be shown Exhibit P 09615.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you have it, sir? No. Do you see the photograph, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me. This is not exactly the way to take testimony, we show a picture and say, "Is this the building?" Mr. Scott is seasoned enough to know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is that the building, sir, from which the shot was fired according to the inquiry that was made?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'd have to see the whole of the area, not just the building itself, because I'm really unable to say to say, in all certainty, whether this is the actual building. It looks like it, but I would have to see the whole area to give you an answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in your opinion, the sniper was right up on the terrace or in a room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the area in which the sniper was, we believe, was the terrace, a short of makeshift building. From the terrace, he was shooting. You cannot see it on this building actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As part of the investigation when you went up to the top of the building, in the course of the investigation did you discover any cartridges on the ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, lots. It was obvious that a sniper had been shooting from there because of the ammunition we found there, the rest of the ammunition we found there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And did the Spanish Battalion have elements of the civilian police or the civil guards who looked for fingerprints and other traces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. When a death occurred, the UN police undertook the investigation. It was a Norwegian police in the case of Lieutenant Munez [phoen]. In the case of Lieutenant Aguilar, I cannot remember the nationality of the police that undertook the investigation, but it was the UN police that undertook the investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm moving to different topic, sir. When you -- you've told us several times in your previous testimony and again today that one of the principal persons you had dealings with on the HVO side was Mr. Bozic. Did Mr. Bozic ever indicate to you in the conversations and meetings that you had with him whether he himself was making the decisions that he conveyed to you or whether those decisions were being made by somebody else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer this question. He never said anything of the sort. And when I say that I maintained conversations, it wasn't me personally who was involved in the talks. Sometimes other members of the command staff were involved, and he never said anything of the sort to me. He said that he was a deputy minister of defence and that he had to consult his superiors, but I cannot answer the question further.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you had occasions to meet with Mr. Bozic or other people at the HVO headquarters -- excuse me, in the HVO, my apologies, can you describe for us where you met these individuals?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, either in the HVO headquarters or in the Spanish headquarters, or we could maintain telephone conversations. The most important or most frequent contacts were over the telephone, but we were certain that the conversations we held with Mr. Bozic were conversations that led to resolving problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you, please, to be shown -- that you be shown, please, Exhibit P 09613. Can you tell us, please, if you recognise that location? Do you have the photograph, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, I think it's the HVO's headquarters or Mostar HVO offices, but I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did you ever have occasion to meet Mr. Bozic at this location?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, I wasn't the person deployed for negotiations when we moved around for negotiations. If at any one time I had to negotiate because I was on duty, it was because I was the only one available.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But if I ever met with him, I never met with him at the general headquarters. I did visit -- visit him, but out of courtesy, and I believe those visits did take place at this office building.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I understand and recall your testimony of the earlier session, Witness BJ, and if not I'm sure I will be corrected, in connection with the testimony you gave about the death of Mr. -- Lieutenant Castellanos. You indicated that you had negotiated, you or people on your staff had negotiated again a mission to take -- to give assistance on the east side and you had negotiated that the day before Lieutenant Castellanos was killed. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, negotiations did take place the day before.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And do you recall who you negotiated or met with or spoke with on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in my previous deposition, I believe I said that I had not participated personally in the agreement. I believe Mr. Praljak had authorised things, but this is mere speculation, because the truth is I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And point, Your Honour, I would make a request that no more questions be put to the witness with respect to this particular issue. I think it's made very clear to us in the last two or three answers that the gentleman, while saying in the past "we," does not necessarily mean he himself participated in negotiations. Therefore I would request that any questions posed this gentleman first be prefaced by whether he, the gentleman, whether he indeed was present or participated in any meetings. If the answer is affirmative, then to proceed. If not, to move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Scott on a number of occasions the witness said he did not attend certain meetings but on each occasion, you went back to the subject. Perhaps you should have asked the witness which meetings he attended, and you should have perhaps avoided mentioning the other ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, with all respect, I think the witness has. There may be some confusion, but the record will speak for itself. The witness has, on a number of occasions, been very clear that he was involved at a number of these events. He said so again today, he said so in June. The record will speak for itself. Secondly, it is quite proper, quite acceptable practice of the Tribunal for the witness to speak about what he knows from what other officers have conveyed to him, his testimony is not limited to his personal knowledge or personal direct involvement. So there's nothing improper about him saying what he knows or what he understands from working with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do agree but it would still be necessary to tell the witness, If you did not attend certain meetings, were you provided with a summary of them, yes or no. If he says no, no one told me about anything, no one summarised anything, then you'd move on to another subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall a dinner meeting with a Bruno Stojic in the summer of 1993, Mr. Stojic and others?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did have dinner with Mr. Stojic not only in summer, also on other occasions. So I don't know which dinner you're referring to specifically, but yes, I did have different on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, can you give us -- can you give the Judges a rough idea how many times you had dinner with Mr. Stojic, then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'd probably make a mistake, but we were in the Croat area, and we always had dinner with the Croat authorities. Whether Mr. Stojic or was not present is something I cannot recall. Maybe two or three. I do not know. It would be mere speculation, but approximately one, two, three. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, you just said now you said you always had dinner with the Croat authorities. "Always" seems to suggest more than one, two, or three occasions. What do you mean? Can you explain to the Judges further? What do you mean when you say, "We always had dinner with the Croat authorities"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if when we arrived in the area, out of politeness we met with the Croat authorities, we visited them in the zone, they might invite us for a coffee, and we in turn, in order to get to know them, invited them to dinner in our barracks. When a Spanish authority, a Spanish general or some other authority came, perhaps we organised dinners to which we invited Croat authorities, and most representative authorities including the commander of the brigade in the area or the mayors, and there were some three or four dinner parties. We're talking about two units that maintained polite relations in the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And did you also invite members of the ABiH, the Bosnia-Herzegovina army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the beginning when they had their headquarters in the western part of Mostar, we did invite them and they did come and we visited them in their general headquarters as we visited the HVO. When they set up or when they were isolated in the eastern area, it was more difficult, but they did come to some meetings and we brought them in our armoured vehicles, but not to a social dinner party, rather, to a working meeting, an important meeting with a view to solving some problems. We did on a number of occasions, in fact, ferry those authorities to our headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Going back to these different meetings, then, do you recall today having one of the dinner meetings with Mr. Stojic on the 18th of July, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically I don't know. I cannot -- I cannot remember specifically whether we had dinner on that date or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'll ask that the witness please be shown Exhibit P 03545. Let me know, sir, when you have that document. It appears to be intrep number 237 dated 18th of July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot find the actual document, the paper document, but if you show it to me perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can we have it put on the screen, please, in e- court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- I could find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Or if not, Your Honour, if I could ask the usher to provide the hard copy to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have found it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, under the heading -- there's a heading called "Other information," and then a number 1. It says: "A dinner was held yesterday with Mr. Bruno Stojic," et cetera. I'd just like you -- would you just look at that passage for a moment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have found that paragraph actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Does that refresh your memory about having a dinner meeting on the 18th of July, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Undoubtedly the dinner did take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And to the best of your recollection, sir, did you attend this dinner?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I would like for you, sir, to look at the report of this meeting. The first item under the general heading I just referred to refers to certain humanitarian issues. There is a second item that says: "Mr. Stojic appeared to be convinced in the capacity of his forces to resolve the situation in their favour once and for all." And you can scan down through the rest of the record of that dinner meeting if you like. Do you have any reason, sir, to doubt the accuracy of this report, of this contemporaneous report made of this meeting on the 18th of July, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Well, first of all, Your Honour, can it be established -- all we know is that the witness said he thinks he was present at the meeting. May it be established whether he recalls hearing anything like this or if it was reported to him by somebody else or at least some basis for the opinion that Mr. Scott is trying to elicit here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Very well. You say that you think you had dinner with Mr. Stojic. Do you happen to remember the discussion at the dinner? What did you talk about during the dinner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot remember that dinner specifically, but if all this is in this document, then all this certainly did take place at that dinner party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, without the document, you wouldn't be able to tell us what actually happened during dinner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, because if I cannot remember the dinner party or the comments, I can say nothing. Once my memory is refreshed via the document, I can say that I do believe that this was talked about at that dinner party because I ascribe a fair deal of reliability to a document drafted by a colleague of mine, but I personally cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, just wrapping up now with a couple of final questions. I'm going to direct your attention back now to the night of the 8th of May, 1993. One might describe it as the night between the 8th and 9th of May, 1993. Were you on duty at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but you're talking about the night between the 8th and the 9th of May. Yes, I was on duty that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I believe you told us in your testimony earlier that you saw a number of military vehicles pass the Spanish Battalion encampment at that time heading in the direction of Mostar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could you tell the Judges, please, at that time could you identify any of the insignia or symbols that were on any of these vehicles that were headed in the direction of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, it was difficult because neither the vehicles nor the battle fatigues were pursuant to duty, and you could not really see the badges or insignia. So I cannot recall what insignias they were carried. I suppose -- I suppose this would be contained in documents. This would be borne out by documents that it could not be clearly seen what insignias or badges were carried.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, finally, sir, in connection with the records and documents at the Spanish Battalion --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour. [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission, in view of this problem -- in view of this problem whether he remembers the details or not, we should take note that in giving his answers, the witness, despite the fact that he's doing his best to try and remember what took place on the basis of the documents, can nonetheless not provide the answer to the question. And it's quite normal if he can't remember, he can't say, but anybody reading the transcript six months later won't be able to realise that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I don't know what to make of that, Your Honour, frankly. The record is what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I think -- I think what Mr. Kovacic was -- was bringing to the Trial Chamber's attention is as follows: A question was posed to the gentleman. The gentleman said that under the conditions he, himself, could not provide an answer. He then went on to say that perhaps it's in the document itself. So at least from this particular witness, we cannot get any answers. Now, as to whether the document itself, whatever is contain in the document is accurate, truthful, and complete, well, it all depends, because then we have to bring in the individual who made that recording, because obviously this gentleman was on duty at that particular day, brought this matter to the attention but is unable to provide any answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think we have this objection now on the record, and that's probably all you -- we need. So we can proceed. Are you agreed?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Good.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Witness BJ --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Witness BJ, when you were here previously in June of this year, in preparing to give your testimony you were asked to look at a large number of documents which I'll represent to you were approximately 274 documents that were organised and presented to you in eight binders. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed. I do recall, and I did -- I did go through all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell us, sir, on the basis of your review, can you tell the Judges whether you were able to determine that all the documents that you reviewed were in fact records or documents of the Spanish army in connection with the Spanish army's mission in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Affirmative. All documents that are actually reviewed during the time of preparation had been produced by the Spanish army and the Canarias and Madrid groups. I also would like to mention here that there were documents that were rejected as not recognised at the time. I had not recognised those documents, as I thought that they -- it could very well have been the case, but I didn't recognise those documents and, therefore, I had to reject them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And do you recall, sir, that when there were certain documents that you rejected, do you recall that those were physically removed from the binders in your presence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Affirmative. At no time during my testimony was I ever questioned on a document that I had rejected.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, can you assist the Judges just generally by indicating some of the various factors that you considered by which you can say that all the documents that you reviewed are Spanish army documents relating to this time period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS  BJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apart from the characteristics of the documents with which I am familiar as pertaining to the type of documents used in the Spanish army, I recognise signatures. I recognise the name of the people who actually wrote those reports both in the terms of the group I belonged to, the people involved, the signatures, the way they compiled those documents, and I have no doubt whatsoever at all who it is written there or stated what they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Witness BJ, on behalf of the Prosecution, I'd like to thank you for your testimony and coming to The Hague on these two occasions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, as far as the time taken, according to the registrar, that was four hours, 30 minutes for the Prosecution. Who is going to confirm that? As I've said, the Defence will have six hours, 45 minutes approximately. It's up to you to decide who's going to start off. Having said that, Mr. Stojic, Petkovic, and Praljak have one hour 30 minutes each, and the others 45 minutes.
